summary: Outlines the process by which the IETF selects an appointment to the Internet Society (ISOC) Board of Trustees. It is a best current practice document about community governance rather than a technical protocol.

eli5.summary: A club that lets another group pick one of its board members needs a fair way to choose. This explains the steps for choosing that person.

subtitle: How the IETF picks the person it names to the Internet Society's Board of Trustees each year.

tldr.problem: The Internet Society (ISOC) by-laws call on the IETF to name 3 Trustees to the ISOC Board, one new Trustee each year, and the IETF needed a defined way to choose them.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB issues a public call for nominations, reviews the nominees and makes a selection, and the IESG confirms it. The process runs on a fixed timeframe so the new Trustee can be seated in June.
tldr.outcome: The IETF has a repeatable, public procedure for this one external appointment, also used for mid-term vacancies, without loading the NomCom with a task it was not built for.

facts.label: New Trustees seated
facts.value: ISOC annual general meeting in June

today: RFC 3677 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 77), and the metadata for this RFC lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. The text reflects the IAB membership and process as of December 2003.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Internet Society (ISOC) provides organizational and financial support for the IETF. ISOC's by-laws call on the IETF to name 3 Trustees to its Board of Trustees (BoT), each with a staggered 3-year term. That means the IETF has to name one Trustee each year.

This memo, a Best Current Practice, describes the process the IETF uses to make that selection. In brief, it sets out the timeframe and procedures for the IAB to solicit public input and make a selection for the open position each year. The same process is used for mid-term vacancies in IETF-nominated Board positions.
sections.eli5: A big group asks a smaller group to choose one board member every year. This note says how the smaller group does the choosing.

sections.title: Why the IAB and Not the NomCom
sections.content:
An alternative would be to use the IETF's Nominating Committee (NomCom, described in RFC 2727). The memo rejects it for two reasons. First, the timeframe of this appointment does not mesh with the IETF appointment cycle. Second, the deliberations and the information solicited would be significantly different for an external appointment such as one to the ISOC BoT.

The text says the timing problem could be solved fairly easily, but the second issue is more general. The NomCom process is oriented toward feedback about individuals and technical positions the community has personal experience with. Judging external appointments would need a different set of skills and might need feedback from outside the IETF, and that side effort could undermine the NomCom's primary task.

By contrast, the IAB is chartered to be responsible for IETF external liaisons, is a standing body that works with ISOC and the ISOC Board, and so already knows what the position needs. The memo leaves open that the IETF might one day broaden the NomCom or create a separate committee for external appointments, but says this is not necessary or desirable for this one annual appointment.
sections.eli5: There is already a team that picks leaders inside the IETF, but this job is different and it is busy. So the team that already talks to outside groups does it instead.

sections.title: Qualifications and Selection Criteria
sections.content:
Candidates should have a demonstrable involvement in the IETF, with a particular focus on active participation in IETF Working Groups. They are expected to have clearly demonstrated technical competence in Internet technology and to be able to explain technology issues so the ISOC Board gets sound technical perspectives. They should also understand the roles and responsibilities of both the IETF and ISOC and be able to explain them in both communities.

A Trustee takes on all the duties of an ISOC Board member: fiduciary responsibility, setting policies, oversight of the operation of the Society, representing the interests of its members and stakeholders, and taking part in all Board meetings and activity programs.

The Trustee is not a representative or delegate of the IETF and is not chartered to represent the IETF or the IETF Standards Process within ISOC. They are, however, expected to call on experts in the IETF community as needed so the Board receives the highest quality technical advice.
sections.eli5: The person chosen should know the IETF well, understand tech, and be ready to do a real board member's job. They speak for themselves, not as the IETF's messenger.

sections.title: Nomination, Selection and Confirmation
sections.content:
Each year the IAB makes a public call for nominations on the ietf-announce@ietf.org mailing list. The call says how nominations are accepted and where the list of nominees will be published. Self-nominations are permitted. Each nomination carries the candidate's name, contact information, and details about their background and qualifications. All IETF participants, including working group chairs, NomCom members, and IAB and IESG members, are eligible.

The IAB publishes the list of nominees, reviews the nomination material and makes a selection. The selection criteria include additional consideration of candidates who are also IAB or IESG members, so that at the time of selection no more than two of the three IETF-appointed Trustees are IAB and IESG members. IAB and IESG members who accept a nomination recuse themselves from the selection and confirmation discussions respectively.

The IESG is the confirming body. If it decides not to confirm the candidate, it gives the IAB the basis for that decision and the IAB nominates another candidate.
sections.eli5: Anyone can suggest a name, even their own. One team picks the best person and a second team checks the pick. If the second team says no, the first team tries again.

sections.title: Timeframe and Mid-term Vacancies
sections.content:
ISOC expects to seat new Board members at its annual general meeting in June each year. The IETF process has three phases, each of 4 to 6 weeks: soliciting nominations; reviewing nominees, deliberating and selecting; and confirmation (with re-selection if needed) and delivery to ISOC. In January the IAB announces the specific dates for that year, taking into account details such as the date of the first IETF meeting of the year.

If an IETF-appointed Trustee cannot serve a full term, the IAB may, at its discretion, immediately select a replacement for the rest of the term using the interim process. In that case a separate timeline is announced and the rest of the process is followed. If the IAB does not use the interim process, the next annual selection fills the vacancy as well as the regular seat.
sections.eli5: The whole thing takes about three rounds of a month or so each, so the new person is ready by June. If someone leaves early, the same steps are used to find a replacement.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says it describes no technical protocols and has no implications for network security. Its Intellectual Property Statement is the standard IETF notice. An appendix lists the IAB members at the time of writing.
sections.eli5: This is a rules-for-people document, not a computer protocol, so there is nothing to hack.
